lessonTitle: Gell and Coombs Types I to IV

blocks.text: A man who has worked with nickel-containing jewellery for years develops an itchy, blistering rash under his watch strap that appears a day or two after wearing it. A second patient's rash appears within minutes of walking through long grass. Both rashes are immune responses, yet they use entirely different machinery and timescales, and sorting them out is the point of the Gell and Coombs classification.

blocks.markdown: **Hypersensitivity** is an excessive or inappropriate adaptive immune response to an antigen that causes tissue damage. The antigen may be foreign (an allergen, a drug, a microbe) or self. In 1963 Gell and Coombs classified reactions into four types by the **effector mechanism**. The classification is a way of thinking about mechanism; real diseases often involve more than one type, and a sensitising first exposure is needed for each.

blocks.title: Hypersensitivity
blocks.text: An immune response that is out of proportion to the threat, or directed against harmless or self antigens, and which causes tissue injury. The effector mechanism defines the type.

rows: IgE bound to mast cells and basophils
Allergic rhinitis (hay fever), atopic asthma, food allergy, anaphylaxis
IgG or IgM against cell-surface or extracellular antigen; complement, phagocytes, NK cells (ADCC)
Mismatched ABO blood transfusion, haemolytic disease of the newborn, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Goodpasture syndrome
Soluble antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissue; complement, neutrophils
Serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, SLE, Arthus reaction
T cells (Th1 with macrophages; CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells)
Contact dermatitis (nickel), tuberculin (Mantoux) reaction, type 1 diabetes, graft rejection
blocks.caption: The four hypersensitivity types

blocks.markdown:
**Type I in detail: the mast cell.** Mast cells and basophils carry the high-affinity IgE receptor **FcεRI**. In **sensitisation**, a first exposure to an allergen drives Th2 cells (IL-4, IL-13) to cause B cells to class-switch to **IgE**, which coats mast cells without causing symptoms. On re-exposure, a multivalent allergen **cross-links** adjacent IgE molecules on the mast cell surface, aggregating FcεRI and triggering signalling that raises intracellular calcium. The sequence is then:

1. **Degranulation (within minutes):** release of preformed mediators, mainly **histamine** (vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, itching) and **tryptase** and other proteases.
2. **Newly synthesised lipid mediators (minutes):** prostaglandin D2 and leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4), which cause prolonged bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.
3. **Cytokines and chemokines (hours):** TNF-α, IL-4, IL-5 and others recruit eosinophils and Th2 cells, producing the **late-phase reaction** 4 to 8 hours after exposure.

blocks.title: Sort the reaction
blocks.prompt: A patient develops hives and wheeze ten minutes after exposure to cat dander. Her skin-prick test is positive. Classify the reaction and describe the sequence of cellular events.

steps.text: Look at timing. A reaction within minutes suggests type I (IgE-mediated).
Confirm mechanism. A positive skin-prick test shows IgE specific for the allergen bound to skin mast cells.
Trace the events. Cat dander allergen cross-links FCεRI-bound IgE, mast cells degranulate, releasing histamine and tryptase, and synthesise leukotrienes and prostaglandin D2.
Explain symptoms. Histamine causes vasodilation and permeability (hives, swelling) and bronchial smooth muscle contraction (wheeze).

blocks.answer: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity; allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, causing degranulation.

blocks.markdown: **Types II, III and IV.** In **type II**, antibody binds antigen on a cell or in tissue, destroying it through complement activation, opsonisation and phagocytosis, or NK-cell ADCC; occasionally antibody alters function without destroying cells (for example stimulating antibodies in Graves disease). In **type III**, antigen and antibody form **soluble immune complexes** that lodge in small blood vessel walls (such as in glomeruli, skin, joints), activate complement and recruit neutrophils, causing inflammation. Complexes form when antibody and antigen are roughly in balance and persist when clearance is impaired. In **type IV**, **T cells** do the damage. Previously sensitised CD4⁺ Th1 cells release IFN-γ and activate macrophages; CD8⁺ cells directly kill cells. There is no antibody involved, which is why the reaction peaks 48 to 72 hours later.

blocks.title: Four questions to classify a reaction
blocks.text: Ask: how quickly did it appear? Is antibody involved or T cells? Is the antigen on a cell surface or soluble? Is the reaction in one place or widely distributed? Minutes and IgE: type I. Antibody to a cell surface: type II. Soluble complexes: type III. T cell and a delay of days: type IV.

blocks.title: Classify these four cases
blocks.prompt: Classify (a) a transfusion reaction with fever and haemoglobinuria ten minutes after the wrong blood group was given; (b) a patient with glomerulonephritis and low C3 two weeks after a throat infection; (c) a red, indurated area 48 hours after intradermal injection of tuberculin protein; (d) a swollen lip 15 minutes after eating a shellfish.

steps.text: (a) The recipient's pre-existing IgM against ABO antigens binds donor red cell surface antigens and activates complement: type II.
(b) Delayed onset after infection with complement consumption suggests deposition of soluble complexes in glomeruli: type III.
(c) A delay of 48 hours in a sensitised person with T cell infiltrate: type IV.
(d) Rapid onset with angioedema after exposure to a food antigen suggests IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation: type I.

items: Type I: IgE, mast cells, minutes (allergic rhinitis).
Type II: antibody against cell-surface or matrix antigen (ABO incompatibility).
Type III: immune complex deposition (serum sickness, SLE).
Type IV: T cell mediated, delayed (contact dermatitis, Mantoux test).

points: The Gell and Coombs classification divides hypersensitivity into types I to IV by effector mechanism.
In type I, IgE-coated mast cells are cross-linked by allergen, degranulate within minutes (histamine) and generate lipid mediators and cytokines for the late phase.
Type II is antibody against cells or tissue, type III is immune complexes, type IV is T cell mediated and delayed.

questions.stem: A reaction begins 10 minutes after exposure to an allergen and is mediated by IgE bound to mast cells. Which hypersensitivity type is this?

distractorRationale.b: Type II is IgG/IgM against cell or matrix antigens.
distractorRationale.c: Type III is immune complex mediated.
distractorRationale.d: Type IV is T cell mediated and delayed.

questions.explanation: Rapid onset and IgE on mast cells define type I hypersensitivity. The other types do not involve IgE as the principal effector.

questions.stem: A hairdresser develops an itchy eczematous eruption on both hands 2 days after starting to use a new hair dye; patch testing is positive for a dye chemical. Which type?

distractorRationale.a: Type I would appear within minutes and is IgE-driven.
distractorRationale.b: Type II involves antibody against cell surface antigens.
distractorRationale.c: Type III involves soluble immune complexes.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: a 48-hour delay and positive patch test indicate T cell-mediated type IV.

questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a classical type IV reaction. Hapten-modified skin proteins are presented to sensitised T cells, which release cytokines and recruit macrophages over 24 to 72 hours.

questions.stem: A patient develops fever, joint pain, rash and proteinuria 9 days after receiving equine antiserum. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Immune complex deposition with complement activation
Cytotoxic T cell killing of the skin

questions.correctOptionText: Immune complex deposition with complement activation

distractorRationale.a: IgE-mediated disease causes acute symptoms within minutes.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: serum sickness is a type III reaction with circulating complexes.
distractorRationale.c: Type IV disease lacks the antibody-driven systemic pattern.
distractorRationale.d: Anti-basement membrane antibody is type II (Goodpasture).

questions.explanation: Serum sickness appears 1 to 2 weeks after exposure to a foreign protein, when antibody forms against circulating antigen and soluble complexes deposit in vessels, joints and kidney.

questions.stem: Which event directly triggers mast cell degranulation in a type I reaction?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aggregation of FcεRI by multivalent allergen triggers signalling and calcium influx.
distractorRationale.c: Perforin is a cytotoxic T cell product.
distractorRationale.d: FcRn transports IgG and does not trigger mast cells.

questions.explanation: The multivalent allergen bridges adjacent IgE molecules bound to FcεRI, aggregating receptors and starting a calcium-dependent signalling cascade leading to degranulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of type II hypersensitivity?

options.text: Haemolytic disease of the newborn due to maternal anti-D antibody

questions.correctOptionText: Haemolytic disease of the newborn due to maternal anti-D antibody

distractorRationale.b: Correct: maternal IgG against fetal red cell antigens destroys the cells.
distractorRationale.c: The Mantoux reaction is type IV.

questions.explanation: In haemolytic disease of the newborn, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, binds antigen on fetal red cells and causes their destruction, a type II mechanism.

questions.stem: True or false: histamine and tryptase are preformed mediators released from mast cells within minutes of cross-linking.
questions.explanation: Mast cell granules contain preformed histamine and proteases such as tryptase, which are released almost immediately. Lipid mediators and cytokines are made later.

questions.stem: An Rh(D)-negative woman (dd) has a child with an Rh(D)-positive man who is heterozygous (Dd). What is the probability, in percent, that a child is Rh(D)-positive and so could be at risk of haemolytic disease if the mother is sensitised?
questions.explanation: The mother can only pass d; the father passes D or d with equal probability. A child is Rh(D)-positive (Dd) with probability 1/2 = 50%. Haemolytic disease is a type II mechanism in which maternal anti-D IgG destroys fetal D-positive red cells.

questions.stem: Describe the sequence of mast cell events in a type I hypersensitivity reaction, from sensitisation to the late phase.
markingGuide: Sensitisation: Th2/IL-4 drives IgE production; IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells
Cytokines recruit eosinophils/Th2 cells: late phase at 4 to 8 hours
questions.explanation: The reaction needs prior sensitisation and then proceeds in minutes, with a second phase hours later.

questions.stem: Give one clinical example of each hypersensitivity type and justify the classification of each by its mechanism.
markingGuide: Type I: allergic rhinitis/anaphylaxis, IgE on mast cells, minutes
Type II: transfusion reaction/haemolytic disease, antibody to cell-surface antigen
Type III: serum sickness/SLE, immune complex deposition
Type IV: contact dermatitis/Mantoux, T cell mediated, 48 to 72 hours
Justification refers to effector, antigen and timing
questions.explanation: Each type has a defining effector mechanism, antigen type and timing, which together classify a reaction.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive skin-prick test to pollen and develops sneezing within minutes of exposure to it. A woman with SLE has glomerulonephritis showing granular immune complex deposits and low C4. Classify each reaction and justify.
markingGuide: First: type I, IgE on mast cells, rapid onset
Second: type III, soluble antigen-antibody complexes deposited in glomeruli with complement consumption (low C4)
Contrast in effector (IgE on mast cells versus complexes with complement) and timing
questions.explanation: Timing and effector cell type separate immediate IgE-mediated reactions from delayed T cell reactions.
